title: Decomposition Detective
tagline: Observation over time · Fair testing · Nature's recycling
goal: Your kid fills a jar with leaves and soil, sets it outside, and turns detective on a mystery that plays out over weeks: what is quietly making these leaves disappear, and why? They record what changes, meet the tiny decomposers doing the work, and run a fair test to find out what speeds it up. By the end, they've seen with their own eyes how a dead leaf becomes the soil that grows the next one.
need: A handful of leaves, a pinch of soil from outside, and a little water
A shaded outdoor spot or windowsill, and a notebook

lesson.text: Decomposition is slow, so the skill is noticing small changes over time. A good observation is dated, specific, and compares to last time.

model.line: The leaves are darker brown, and two have holes in them.
They feel soft and floppy, not crunchy.
Since Day 5: white fuzz has appeared on the bottom leaf.

lesson.modelNote: 'Different' gives next week nothing to compare. The fix has a date, a look, a feel and what's new since Day 5.

howTo.intro: The hard part is the waiting. Build the jar, leave it alone, and look a few times a week. Keep the lid loose, look at mould through the glass instead of sniffing it, and wash hands after each check.

plan.what: The rot-or-not sort, build both jars, record Day One (Steps 1, 2 and 4). 30 minutes.
Look 2 or 3 times a week and compare the two jars (Steps 3 and 4). 5 minutes each.
Close the case and report the findings (Step 5).

troubleshoot.a: Normal for the first week. Check it's damp (not wet) and not sealed tight. Around week two, things speed up.
Too wet or sealed. Open it up, add a few dry leaves, and give it air. Decomposers need to breathe too.
Bring the jar inside to a cool, shaded spot. Below freezing the decomposers stop, and a damp glass jar can crack.

steps.title: Sort rot or not
steps.why: A quick prediction game, then the jar gets built.
steps.kid: Gather a few small things: a leaf, a scrap of paper, a bit of apple, a plastic bottle cap, a pebble. Your kid sorts them into two piles, 'nature will break it down' and 'it won't,' and says why. Then they build the time capsule: a clear jar with a handful of leaves, a pinch of outdoor soil and a splash of water, damp but not soaking, loosely covered so it can breathe. They push one thing from each pile against the glass: the paper, a bit of apple, the bottle cap.
steps.you: Ask why for each guess, and don't mark anything wrong yet: they'll check later. Help with the jar, then hand it fully to them. Put it somewhere shaded where they'll remember to look. Paper was once a tree, which is why it rots.
ask: Which of these do you think nature can break down?
Why do you think we added soil, and not just leaves?
steps.tip: The soil is the secret ingredient. It carries the tiny living things that do the breaking down.

levels.explore: Sort 3 objects, then build one simple jar.
levels.develop: Sort 6 objects with a reason each, then build and label the jar.
levels.extend: Sort again by 'was it once alive?' Does that rule predict rot better than your first guess?

steps.title: Record Day One
steps.why: Your kid captures the starting point, before anything changes.
steps.kid: Your kid draws the jar exactly as it looks today and writes a few words on the colour, size and feel of the leaves. This is the 'before' every experiment needs. Without it, they can't prove anything changed.
steps.you: Write the date at the top together. It feels dull because nothing has happened yet, and that's exactly why it matters.
ask: What colour and size are the leaves right now?
Soft or crunchy? Wet or dry?
steps.tip: A photo of the jar on Day One, next to the drawing, makes the final comparison really satisfying.

levels.develop: A sketch plus a written description.
levels.extend: Tape-mark the leaf layer's height on the jar so shrinking becomes a number.

steps.title: Watch it change
steps.why: Two or three times a week, your kid records what's different.
steps.kid: Your kid checks the jar a few times a week and writes a dated entry like the example: what it looks like, how the leaves feel, and what changed since last time. The leaves darken, soften and grow fuzz, and the thinnest bits start to fall apart. When a week barely changes, they write that too.
steps.you: Help them remember (a note on the fridge works). Before each look, ask them to predict what they'll find. Then introduce the culprits: decomposers, tiny fungi, bacteria and bugs eating the leaves and turning them into nutrients for plants. For Extend: most of a missing leaf leaves as carbon dioxide the decomposers breathe out.
ask: What looks different from last time? What stayed the same?
Who do you think is doing the work in this jar?
steps.tip: 'No visible change' counts as data, not a failure. White or green fuzz is mould, one of the decomposers: the jar is working.

levels.explore: Notice one change after a week.
levels.develop: Record dated changes across several weeks, using the word decomposer.
levels.extend: The leaves are shrinking. Where did the missing leaf go?

steps.title: Run the fair test
steps.why: Two jars, one difference, and a real question.
steps.kid: Your kid sets up two jars that are the same except for one thing. Moisture is a great first test: Jar A dry, Jar B damp. Or they pick their own: warm versus cool, torn leaves versus whole. They predict which will break down faster, then compare the two jars each time they look.
steps.you: Build the second jar on Day 1 so both start together; the Step 1 jar can be one of the pair. Hold them to changing just one thing. Let their prediction lead the test, even if it's not the one you'd pick.
ask: What's the one thing we're changing between the jars?
Which do you predict will break down faster, and why?
steps.tip: This is the leap from watching nature to questioning it. They're asking a question and reading the answer.

levels.develop: Describe the difference between the two jars with dated notes.
levels.extend: Before looking, decide what counts as 'faster', so the result can't be bent.

steps.title: Close the case
steps.why: Your kid reports what they found, with weeks of notes behind it.
steps.kid: Your kid writes or tells their findings: what broke down and what didn't (back to the rot-or-not sort), what made it faster or slower, and the big idea that nature is constantly recycling dead things into the soil that grows new life. They point to their drawings and jars as evidence.
steps.you: Take the report seriously: they earned it with weeks of watching. Then tip the jar into a pot, plant a seed in it together, and let the decomposers keep working while it grows.
ask: Which of your rot-or-not guesses were right?
If a friend asked why leaves disappear in the fall, what would you tell them?
steps.tip: A seed planted in the jar's soil and leaves shows where all that rotting is headed.

levels.develop: Write a short conclusion with evidence from your notes.
levels.extend: Name one thing that could have fooled your test, like more sun on one jar, and how you'd rule it out.

conclusion.headline: Case closed: they know where the leaves went.
conclusion.text: Turn over the leaf pile under a tree together and find a soft, dark leaf with holes in it. They can tell you what's breaking it down, and why the bottom layer is further along than the top.
conclusion.celebrate: The day the leaves first feel soft instead of crunchy, say: 'You've checked this jar for weeks, and you caught the moment it changed.'
extensions: Start a real compost bin and track kitchen scraps turning into soil
Bury a few objects in the yard and dig them up months later
Race a sealed bag against an open pile
Plant a seed in the jar's soil and leaves

signs: They notice rotting logs and leaf piles on walks
They write dated notes and compare to last time
They want to test their own 'what if' ideas
makeItReal: Start a family compost: decide together what goes in, who turns it, and where the finished soil goes in the spring. Let them be the one who checks whether it's too dry.

onTheRoad: Turn over the leaf litter in a forest here and compare how thick, damp and broken down it is with home.
Tuck one leaf under a stone in a damp spot and another in a dry spot, and check both before you move on.
Ask, with your help, what local families do with food scraps here, like compost, animals or a bin, and why.
backHome: Set up a second jar in the warmest, dampest spot you can find at home, and test the prediction from the trip.
